text:
Alaska Shock: Senator Toppled By RCV Twist

https://t.co/ajb2A6JO3E
Alaska’s Senate flip turns on something more durable than one news cycle: how a ranked-choice system and a fractured Republican field met a coalition-ready Democrat with deep statewide roots—and produced a clear, rules-aligned win.
At a Glance

Democrat Mary Peltola defeated incumbent Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan for Alaska’s U.S. Senate seat, flipping it to Democrats.
Official Alaska Division of Elections tallies placed Peltola first in the statewide count; subsequent projections called the race for her.
Alaska’s ranked-choice system blunted any spoiler effect from similarly named candidates and reinforced Peltola’s advantage.
The outcome reflects Alaska’s post-2020 election architecture: open primaries, ranked-choice voting, and coalition-friendly politics.
What the results show and why they held
The decisive fact is straightforward: Democrat Mary Peltola finished ahead of two-term Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan in the statewide count, with the Alaska Division of Elections reporting Peltola at 141,637 votes (49.98%) to Sullivan’s 130,162 (45.93%), in a 283,377-vote contest. The margin—11,475 votes—made her the frontrunner heading into final tabulation and prompted major outlets to project the seat for Peltola, confirming one of the election’s most consequential flips in a state long considered right of center at the federal level.
Ranked-choice voting (RCV), now the backbone of Alaska’s general elections, mattered less as a late twist than as the structural context for the entire race. RCV requires a candidate to cross a majority threshold via sequential redistribution of lower-ranked choices if no one clears 50% on first preferences. In this contest, Peltola’s first-choice lead and the transfer patterns implied by public data meant that even if she finished a hair under 50% on first count, she was well-positioned to prevail on transfers—particularly given how nonmajor-party and similarly named candidates’ ballots tended to break.
Mechanics: how Alaska’s ranked-choice system shaped the outcome
Alaska adopted open primaries and RCV by ballot initiative in 2020; the state’s high court later upheld the framework, cementing it as the rule set for subsequent cycles. In practice, voters can rank multiple candidates, and if no one wins an outright majority in round one, the last-place finisher is eliminated and their votes are redistributed to the next-ranked candidate on each ballot; the process repeats until a candidate surpasses 50%.

Two dynamics in this Senate race rewarded coalition breadth over base intensity. First, a second “Dan Sullivan” (Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.) appeared on the ballot; his small share of first-choice votes raised tactical questions but did not eclipse Peltola’s lead when combined with the incumbent’s total. Second, analyses of Alaska’s prior RCV behavior and available election files indicated that a meaningful share of voters who selected the similarly named candidate also ranked Peltola second, a pattern that, under RCV, would tend to consolidate her advantage rather than spoil it. In other words, the system’s design absorbed potential confusion and converted it into transfers, not chaos.

The vote math: what was needed and what actually happened
Peltola’s first-choice share sat just at the cusp of a majority—effectively 50% on a 283,000-vote base—which is why projections were aggressive even before formal tabulation rounds were complete. The arithmetic favored her two ways. If late-counted ballots nudged her above 50%, she would win outright. If not, elimination rounds were likely to add to her total, not subtract from it, based on observed transfer behavior in earlier Alaska races and the specific mix of minor candidates in this field.

The incumbent’s path required either an improbable late surge from uncounted ballots concentrated in reliably Republican precincts or an unusually favorable transfer pattern from eliminated candidates’ ballots that overcame a five-figure deficit. Neither materialized at scale. Outlets subsequently called the race, and reporting from national and Alaska-focused desks aligned with the state’s data releases.

Why this flip was plausible in Alaska’s political ecosystem
The result is less an ideological whiplash than a lesson in how Alaska’s reengineered electoral incentives favor candidates who can harvest cross-partisan second choices. Peltola had already demonstrated that capacity in her 2022 special House victory, where she assembled a coalition that withstood late transfers from Republican-leaning voters. The 2026 Senate contest replayed that script: a Democrat with broad personal appeal and a reputation for Alaska-first pragmatism facing a divided Republican field under RCV rules that reward depth of support beyond first preferences.

That architecture also curbs classic spoiler risk. In a plurality system, a same-named challenger might split an incumbent’s base irretrievably. Under RCV, those ballots are not lost; if voters rank the incumbent second, their preferences flow back upon the challenger’s elimination. Where voters instead ranked Peltola second, the mechanism reflects actual voter intent—an argument for RCV’s resilience in the face of strategic candidacies and ballot-order idiosyncrasies documented by election scholars.

The “two Dan Sullivans” controversy and the rule of law
Late-campaign attention centered on allegations that Democrats recruited a similarly named candidate to siphon votes from the incumbent. Whatever the political theater, the legal and structural guardrails mattered more: the state’s RCV system mitigates misfire outcomes, the courts have affirmed Alaska’s authority to run its elections under this framework, and federal attempts to preemptively condition certification on a specific candidate’s victory were rejected as inconsistent with constitutional allocations of power to the states.

Put plainly, the system performed as designed. Voters could rank candidates; election officials followed statutory timelines for late-arriving absentee processing and tabulation; and when projections arrived, they reflected the combined effect of first-choice tallies and predictable transfer behavior under established law.

Consequences: what this means for governance and future campaigns
Peltola’s win expands Democrats’ Senate margin and gives Alaska a senator whose coalition was built as much on second-choice acceptability as first-choice fervor. That has implications for how she will govern—coalition-built winners tend to prize cross-aisle relationships—and for how challengers will campaign. Republican strategists in Alaska now face a strategic imperative: either consolidate the field before November or court second-choice rankings aggressively, because in an RCV regime, alienating adjacent blocs is a losing proposition even when base turnout is strong.

For reformers elsewhere, Alaska’s cycle offers two takeaways. First, RCV can reduce the payoff from cynical duplicate-name gambits or narrowcasting strategies that bank on plurality wins. Second, voter education remains essential. The system does not require a voter to rank multiple candidates, but ranking sincerely expands a ballot’s influence across rounds and more fully captures voter intent—an effect visible in the transfer math that underwrote Peltola’s advantage.
The bottom line
Mary Peltola’s ouster of a sitting Republican senator in Alaska is not a paradox; it is the anticipated product of a modernized election system meeting a candidate suited to it. The data from the state, the logic of ranked choice, and the projection calls point the same direction: a clear, rules-consistent result that turns a long-red seat blue and will shape how both parties approach Alaska for cycles to come.

text:
I WAS NEVER CALLED TO RESCUE THE CHURCH. I WAS CALLED TO SERVE THE PEOPLE.

So, with my health failing, my depression and CPTSD raging, my feet all messed up, and the crippling pain I live with in my spine and other parts of my body, how much more proof do you need to see that I am called to be a missionary?

Think about it.

At the height of my mission, it wasn't people who destroyed my world. I cancelled myself years ago, lol. I wasn't chasing fame, attention or recognition. I was simply out there speaking my message, walking into the fields and serving people. Walking, something I can barely do physically anymore.

I never sought attention as someone who became well known. I never allowed videos to be taken of me speaking. I always made it about the people, never about myself. And because of that, I was welcomed into practically every culture, race and faith you can imagine.

Then something happened.

Women were being rescued from human trafficking. Teenagers were getting clean from deadly drugs. People were discovering a non-judgemental understanding of faith. People were finding hope, purpose and a different way of looking at life.

And while all this was happening, I was happy. Truly happy.

I wasn't rich financially. I was broke. But I was rich in my heart because I knew I was leaving behind a better legacy.

And yet, while all this was happening out in the world, much of the church couldn't see it or understand it. They seemed more interested in entertainment, performances and putting on a show to make attending church exciting.

Meanwhile, I was going to war alone, with the help of just a couple of people over the years.

Have I screwed up? Absolutely. Plenty of times. I'm not an easy person to be friends with, and I never claimed to be. But I fight a war that most people will never understand.

There is the personal war I fight every single day, and then there is the war I fight to help save others from the life I once lived and to help them find their way away from destruction and towards God.

This isn't entertainment to me. I know exactly what I was saved from. I give a damn about people. All people.

And perhaps it is because I care so much that my world has come under attack. I don't have an army of soldiers standing beside me in the battle. Instead, I have people who would rather blame me, question whether I'm holy enough, or tell me they don't like hearing the message coming from somebody with my background.

But do you know who DOES like hearing from me?

The thousands upon thousands of people I have spoken to, worked with and stood alongside over the years.

I don't say that out of vanity. Please don't mistake it for that. I'm making a point.

I was never called to rescue the church. I was called to serve the people.

And you cannot do that by sitting behind church walls, entertaining yourself in a pew and waiting for somebody else to do the dirty work.

You have to get out there. You have to get your hands dirty. You have to meet people where they are, not where you think they should be.

So, if I'm suffering now, I can at least look back and know that I gave everything I had to the job. I did it with my whole heart.

And I believe there is a spiritual battle taking place. I feel like the enemy is having a field day with me. And because I refuse to participate in praising the church, its institutions or its vanity instead of focusing on the people, I often find myself fighting alone.

Christians will tell you that there are no coincidences with God.

Well, I have a question.

If that is true, then perhaps we should think about the timing of everything. At the height of my mission, when I was out there serving, reaching people and seeing lives change, my physical and mental health began taking me down. Not people. Not critics. Not those who wanted to destroy my reputation. My own body and mind began failing me.

And now I find myself unable to do physically what I spent so many years doing.

If Christians aren't willing to stand behind somebody who has dedicated his life to serving others, and help provide that person with the tools and support needed to continue the work, then I have to ask myself whether I'm representing the wrong faith.

Don't misunderstand me. I have some lovely Christian friends, and I will never turn my back on God.

But Christianity is struggling, and there is a reason other faiths, including Islam, are growing so rapidly around the world. People are looking for God. They're looking for faith, genuine relationships, authenticity and a sense of belonging.

They want something real.

Yet too often, Christianity seems more concerned with membership numbers, maintaining the congregation it already has and finding new ways to entertain people.

This isn't an attack. It's an observation, and I believe it's one that needs to be made.

Think about it. If your pastor started getting sick, experiencing crippling pain and struggling mentally and physically, how many people would rush to pray for him? How many would offer assistance, visit him, bring him what he needed or simply sit beside him?

Now consider the servant who spent years out in the field, putting his entire life into serving others, and actually seeing the fruits of that labour.

What happens when that person becomes sick and needs help?

Suddenly, he becomes invisible.

Since I began experiencing these physical and mental battles over the past few years, how many Christians have actually come to sit with me, pray with me or simply visit me?

Think about that.

Of the thousands of Christians I have encountered over the years, how many have genuinely had my back without me having to beg, plead or reach absolute rock bottom before somebody notices?

I have a couple of friends whom I see every few months, and I appreciate them. But where is everybody else?

Yes, God sees everything. And I believe there will come a day when we all have to answer for how we treated one another.

I've been part of crews and gangs in my former life. I know what brotherhood means. You put in the work. You earn trust. You stand beside one another when things get ugly. You don't just walk around calling everybody brother because it sounds good.

And Christianity shouldn't be any different when it comes to genuine brotherhood and sisterhood.

I put in the work. I went into the field. I saw the results. I watched people change their lives. I served people who might never have stepped foot inside a church.

But I didn't do it for church membership, applause or recognition. I did it because people mattered.

So, from this point forward, I will never call someone a Christian brother or sister simply because they attend church, quote scripture or know how to talk a good game.

I want to see the work. I want to see the compassion. I want to see the willingness to stand beside somebody when there is nothing to gain and everything to give.

Because otherwise, you're just a chin-wagging clown, a jester, an entertainer.

You might know how to put on a good show, but that doesn't make you a missionary.

THE MISSION WAS NEVER ABOUT FILLING PEWS. IT WAS ABOUT CHANGING LIVES.

And I would rather spend one day in the trenches making a difference than spend a lifetime sitting in a pew being entertained.

text:
Saul believed might come from keeping the animals, the LORD had not authorized the exception. Whatever explanation he offered concerning the people’s participation, the commandment had already established what was required. Whatever religious value he attached to the surviving livestock, the terms of obedience had not changed. A man cannot rewrite yesterday’s commandment by producing today’s explanation. He cannot make a prohibited action acceptable simply because circumstances have created an opportunity to defend it. This principle is especially important wherever religious language is involved. People often speak as though a good intention supplies sufficient authority for an action, but a good intention cannot override a clear command of God. The question is never merely whether a proposed result sounds desirable. The question is whether the means used to obtain it are consistent with Scripture. Saul was about to demonstrate how confidently a man can claim obedience when he has already decided to make exceptions for himself.

Chapter II — The Evidence That Survived the Battle

Saul did not ignore the entire assignment. He gathered the army, organized the campaign, and advanced against Amalek. He warned the Kenites to depart because they had shown kindness to the children of Israel, and the Kenites separated themselves from the Amalekites before the attack. The campaign proceeded, and the Amalekites suffered a devastating defeat. Those facts are important because they explain how Saul could return from battle with the appearance of having successfully accomplished what God required. There had been real military action, real danger, and real results. The king had not remained comfortably at home while refusing to undertake the mission. He had led an army against the enemy and carried out substantial portions of the commandment. Yet visible accomplishment is not the same thing as faithfulness to every requirement of a particular assignment. The narrative does not invite us to dismiss everything Saul did merely because he failed at the decisive point. It invites us to examine how a record containing genuine accomplishments could become the foundation for a claim that was not true. Saul had enough military success to make his announcement sound impressive. That success, however, could not erase the difference between what God commanded and what Saul permitted to survive.

The ninth verse of 1 Samuel 15 supplies the evidence that would later confront the king. Scripture records that Saul and the people spared Agag, along with the best sheep, oxen, fatlings, lambs, and everything they regarded as good. The same verse explains that they destroyed what was vile and refuse. The distinction was not accidental. The desirable livestock was preserved while the undesirable portion was destroyed. The commandment had not established that division. Saul and the people had made it. Notice that the animals were not described as escaping from the battlefield or surviving through circumstances beyond Saul’s control. The Bible says they were spared. That word establishes responsibility. The decision to preserve them was part of the very conduct later exposed by Samuel. There is no need to invent an unrecorded discussion among the soldiers, imagine a secret agreement with Agag, or pretend to know the precise financial calculations behind the decision. The passage provides sufficient information to establish the wrongdoing. They preserved what God had commanded them not to spare. The animals therefore became direct physical evidence of an incomplete and disobedient campaign. Their survival was not a minor historical curiosity. It contradicted the assignment itself and would soon contradict the king’s public testimony concerning that assignment.

text:
Tarik Skubal turns 30 today, and the New York Mets spent his birthday offering him nine years and almost $400 million.

Jim Duquette put the number on MLB Network. It is an opening bid and nothing is signed. Scott Boras is still taking calls from the Dodgers, the Blue Jays and the Padres.

Nine years at just under $400 million comes out around $44 million a season.

The record for a pitcher is $43.33 million a year. Max Scherzer and Justin Verlander share it.

Both of them signed those deals with the Mets. The Mets then traded both of them away inside three days at the 2023 deadline, Scherzer to Texas on the 30th of July and Verlander back to Houston two days after that.

So the Mets are offering to break a pitcher record they set themselves, twice, with two men they then got rid of.

The biggest guarantee any pitcher has signed is Yoshinobu Yamamoto's, twelve years and $325 million. Skubal spent the last two months of this season in the same rotation as him.

That arm has been operated on three times.

Tommy John came after his 2015 college season and cost him most of 2016 and all of 2017. In August 2022 it was a flexor tendon repair in his left forearm. This past May they went in to clear loose bodies out of his elbow, and he was back on a mound by the 13th of June.

Jason Beck at https://t.co/JE0Vt6pI6E never reported that all three were the same joint, and nobody here is going to claim it either. All that is on the record is that all three were his pitching arm.

In 2017, with that elbow still rebuilding, the Arizona Diamondbacks drafted him in the 29th round. He said no and went back to school.

A year later Detroit took him in the ninth round, 255th overall, and handed him a signing bonus of $350,000.

His first big league salary, back in 2020, was $563,500. This season he made $32 million. Add up every dollar FanGraphs has him earning from 2020 through this year and you land a little over $48 million.

The first year of the Mets offer would pay him almost all of that again.

Nobody had put a number in front of him yet when Matt Snyder at CBS asked about free agency on the 15th of October, in a visiting dugout in Los Angeles, with the Brewers finishing off the Dodgers behind him.

"I'm not going to comment on my future really at all," he said. "Today sucks, you know, and that's kind of where my head's at."

Five weeks later the 29th round pick who said no turns 30, and the number sitting in front of him is bigger than any pitcher has ever signed for.

text:
When the power goes out, most of us assume it’ll be back in 20 minutes. Sometimes it is. Sometimes it’s two days, and the groceries are on the line.

Here’s what food safety experts at the FDA and USDA say:
~A closed refrigerator keeps food safe for about 4 hours.
~A full freezer holds its temperature for about 48 hours, and a half-full one for about 24, as long as the door stays shut.
~When in doubt, throw it out. If perishable food like meat, milk or leftovers sits above 40 degrees for more than 2 hours, it’s not worth the risk.

Keep the doors closed. Every peek lets cold air out.

That full fridge and freezer can easily hold hundreds of dollars in food, so a little preparation saves real money:
~Keep a cooler and a few frozen water bottles or ice packs on hand.
~Put an appliance thermometer in your fridge and freezer so you know whether food stayed cold.
~Check your homeowners or renters insurance. Some policies cover food spoilage, but often only with an add-on or after a deductible.
~Ask your utility whether it offers credits or claims for long outages.

Here in Colorado, Xcel Energy has also used planned shutoffs during high winds and wildfire danger. Sign up for your utility’s outage alerts so you get a heads-up.

And a few safety basics:
~Keep flashlights and batteries where you can find them in the dark. Skip the candles.
~Charge phones and a backup battery when bad weather is coming.
~If anyone in your home relies on electricity for medical equipment, tell your utility and have a backup plan.
~Never run a generator indoors, in a garage, or near windows and doors. Carbon monoxide is invisible and deadly.

An emergency fund protects your bank account. An emergency kit protects everything else.

I’m not a financial advisor.

Sources: FDA, USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service, CDC, Xcel Energy
